title: Game Selection Is the Strategy Before the Strategy
author: Admired Leadership
summary: The Admired Leadership newsletter argues that the most consequential strategic decision a leader makes is not how to play the game they're in but which game to play in the first place. Using the Genghis Khan example -- the Mongols did not try to compete on European feudal terms but selected a game (cavalry-based rapid movement) that neutralized European advantages and maximized their own -- the piece develops the concept of 'game selection' as a meta-strategic capability. The argument is that most strategic planning takes the competitive context as given and optimizes within it, when the most powerful strategic move is often to change the context itself. The piece offers a framework for game selection: identify which assumptions your current strategy takes as fixed, test whether any of those assumptions could be changed, and determine whether changing them would shift the competitive dynamics in your favor. The piece is particularly relevant for leaders in industries undergoing structural disruption, where the old rules of the game may no longer apply.
points: * Game selection -- choosing which competitive context to operate in -- is a meta-strategic capability that precedes and supersedes conventional strategy, which takes the context as given and optimizes within it. * The Genghis Khan example illustrates that the most powerful strategic move is often to change the competitive context rather than to optimize within it: the Mongols did not try to beat European armies at their own game. * Most strategic planning treats competitive context as fixed, asking 'how do we win?' when the prior question is 'is this a game we should be playing, and if not, what game should we select?' * The game selection framework asks: which assumptions does our current strategy take as fixed? Could any of those assumptions be changed? Would changing them shift competitive dynamics in our favor? * The framework is most valuable during structural disruption, when the old rules may no longer be optimal and the question of which game to play becomes more urgent than the question of how to play better.
quotes: Genghis Khan didn't try to compete on European feudal terms. He didn't build castles. He didn't train knights. He didn't try to beat the Europeans at the game they had spent centuries designing and optimizing. He played a completely different game -- cavalry-based rapid movement, siege avoidance, supply-chain disruption -- that neutralized everything they were good at.

Most strategic planning asks: how do we win the game we're in? Game selection asks: is this the right game? Should we be competing here, in this way, under these rules? The question sounds obvious when you state it plainly. It is almost never asked.

The assumptions that your strategy takes as fixed are the most important thing to audit. Which customers are we trying to serve? Which channels do we consider viable? Which cost structures do we accept as given? Which regulatory environment do we treat as permanent? Every one of those is a choice, and choices can be changed.

The best strategic move of the last decade in almost every industry has been made by a company that decided not to play the incumbent's game. They changed the unit of value, the distribution model, the cost structure, the customer definition -- and then they competed. The incumbents had better strategies in the wrong game.

The meta-question -- which game should we play? -- is harder than the ordinary strategic question because it requires questioning assumptions that have become invisible through familiarity. The very fact that an assumption is rarely examined is evidence that it might be worth examining.
